intro:
Italian restaurant phone orders can pile up fast, especially at dinner, weekends, and holidays. An AI phone host can answer those calls, take the order, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen.

That matters for pizza shops, pasta spots, delis, and family restaurants that already know the phone rings when the room gets busy. ROAL is built for that job: it answers calls, takes pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and hands off harder calls to staff.

sections.h2: What should an AI phone host say on an Italian restaurant order call?
sections.body:
For Italian restaurant phone orders, the host should sound simple and direct. It should ask for the name, number, pickup or delivery, and then walk through the order in the same way your staff would.

A good script keeps the call moving:
- “Thanks for calling. Is this for pickup or delivery?”
- “What can I start for you today?”
- “Any sizes, toppings, sides, or notes?”
- “What name and phone number should I put on the order?”
- “Your total is about $28, and it will be ready at 6:20.”

For an Italian menu, that matters because callers often order many small details. The host should capture items, sizes, modifiers, and notes, then repeat the order back before ending the call. If a caller asks for something sold out, it should not offer it. If the question is tricky, it should pass the call to staff with a short summary.

sections.h2: Which Italian menu details need the most care?
sections.body:
Italian menus often have many custom parts, so the order flow needs to be tight. Think about pasta shape, sauce choice, portion size, toppings, and add-ons like bread, salad, or extra protein.

Use a quick checklist for your menu setup:
- Pasta: spaghetti, penne, rigatoni, or whatever you serve
- Sauce: marinara, vodka sauce, Alfredo, pesto, and specials
- Sizes: small, large, half tray, full tray, or your own names
- Modifiers: extra cheese, no onion, light sauce, gluten-sensitive note
- Notes: “on the side,” “well done,” “cut into squares,” or “no garlic”

If your menu changes often, make sure the live menu matches what you can actually make that day. ROAL reads menu pages, PDFs, and even menu photos, and the owner can update details later in the dashboard. That helps keep phone orders close to what your kitchen is already serving.

sections.h2: How do pickup and delivery phone orders fit into a busy dinner rush?
sections.body:
Dinner rush is where phone orders can get messy. One person answers, another is packing orders, and a third is trying to keep tickets straight. A phone host helps by taking the order, quoting the ready time, and sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

Here is a simple workflow you can use:
1. Forward calls when busy or unanswered.
2. Let the host take the order from the live menu.
3. Confirm the name, phone, and ready time.
4. Check the kitchen screen for the ticket.
5. Hand off only the calls your staff needs to handle.

Worked example: say your average Italian pickup order is $28. If you get 15 completed phone orders in a night, that is $420 in order volume. Plug in your own average ticket and order count to see what phone ordering is worth for your shop. ROAL charges per completed phone order, so you only pay when a confirmed order reaches the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: How much does phone answering cost compared with other options?
sections.body:
It helps to compare the common ways restaurants handle calls. Delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call. Many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, even in slow weeks.

Here is a simple comparison table you can use with your own numbers:

| Option | Common cost style | Good fit | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Delivery apps | Commission per order | More online visibility | High fees on each order |
| Human answering | Per minute or per call | Lots of overflow calls | Cost can rise with busy nights |
| Monthly AI phone tools | Fixed monthly fee | Predictable billing | You pay even when calls are light |
| ROAL | $0.90 per completed phone order | Phone orders, pickup, delivery, questions | Not for taking card numbers over the phone |

For many Italian restaurants, the useful question is not “What is the cheapest?” but “What costs less than losing a call?” That is why it helps to track your average order size, how often the phone rings, and how many calls your team misses during rushes.

sections.h2: How do I forward my restaurant number without losing it?
sections.body:
You can keep your existing restaurant number and forward calls to the phone host when you want. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered.

A practical setup checklist:
- Keep your main number on the sign, menu, and website
- Forward calls only during rush hours if that fits your shop
- Test the forwarding from a real phone before going live
- Turn forwarding off any time if you need to

Phone forwarding codes vary by carrier and plan, so confirm with your provider and test with a call. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 forwards calls and *73 turns it off. On some mobile carriers, codes like **21*number# or **61*number# may be used, while Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73 and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set this in the web portal. If you want a quick reference, see [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.body:
Setup is quick and does not need a long IT project. An owner pastes their restaurant website, Google Maps link, or name and city into /try. ROAL reads the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages, then builds a phone host in about a minute.

Typical setup steps:

2. Review the menu, hours, and address it finds.
3. Test-call it in the browser, no sign-up needed.
4. Claim the host when you are ready.
5. Forward your existing number to it.

You can also upload a menu in any format. The owner picks the voice and name, and questions the host cannot answer go to an inbox. Answer them once, and the host learns it for later calls. If you want to compare plan structure before you start, see [pricing](/pricing).

sections.h2: What should staff handle instead of the phone host?
sections.body:
A good phone host should take the routine calls and pass the sensitive ones to people. That keeps your team available for real restaurant issues while still helping callers quickly.

Send these to staff with a summary:
- Catering requests
- Complaints
- Allergy-sensitive questions
- Manager requests
- Anything the host cannot answer from the menu or FAQ

Example handoff line: “Caller wants a gluten-sensitive order for pickup at 7:15 and asked to confirm with a manager.”

One important limit: the host does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it. That keeps the phone flow simple and avoids trying to force every call into the same pattern.
